candidateRows: Atheism cannot be lived in an ideologically pure form because ordinary life relies on faith-like principles external to materialist nature and evolutionary biology.
This is Shapiro's foundational formulation of the atheist-delusion thesis and establishes the extra-natural assumptions on which his case against self-sufficient secular life depends.
After the moderator introduces the social role of religion and asks for a concise account of the atheist delusion, Shapiro lays out his principal case before O'Connor responds.
Although a godless universe precludes free will, adding God does not make free will intelligible and therefore cannot solve the underlying problem.
The objection directly contests the claimed asymmetry between atheism and theism by arguing that the extra-natural hypothesis fails to explain the very phenomenon invoked against atheism.
Shapiro's claim that free will cannot arise in a purely materialist or Darwinian universe.
Immediately after Shapiro's opening thesis, O'Connor accepts the incompatibility of atheism and free will but disputes the suggestion that theism supplies a solution.
Determinism does not imply passivity, because human beings still act from biological and psychological drives even though they do not freely choose those drives.
This response blocks the practical-behavioral objection to determinism by explaining how ordinary motivated action remains expected when conduct is causally driven rather than freely authored.
Shapiro's contention that O'Connor professes disbelief in free will but does not live or behave accordingly.
Following Shapiro's claim that O'Connor does not act as though free will is absent, O'Connor explains the Schopenhauerian distinction between acting on desires and choosing desires.
A functional society needs widespread belief in meaningful agency because people behave and improve more effectively when they believe their choices matter.
The move connects the metaphysical free-will dispute to the debate's social-order motion, arguing that belief in agency has indispensable motivational and behavioral consequences.
O'Connor's account of human action as the determined product of biological and evolutionary drives.
After O'Connor explains why determinism does not keep people in bed, Shapiro shifts from metaphysical possibility to purpose, behavioral evidence, and social functionality.
Free will is logically impossible because any mental event is either determined or undetermined, leaving action controlled by prior causes or by randomness even if a soul exists.
This is O'Connor's principal positive argument against free will and is designed to apply equally to material minds, immaterial minds, and souls, undermining theistic rescue attempts.
Shapiro's claim that lived purpose and socially beneficial agency point beyond deterministic evolutionary explanation.
O'Connor answers the appeal to purpose by treating the experience of agency as an evolved illusion, then grounds his denial of free will in a determined-or-random dilemma.
The determined-or-random argument wrongly decomposes the self, since the self is fundamentally a unified deciding being rather than merely an assemblage of non-deciding mechanisms.
The response attacks a key premise of O'Connor's logical case by defending an irreducible conception of the deciding self and denying its compatibility with reductive atheism.
O'Connor's determined-or-undetermined dilemma purporting to show that no self or soul can exercise free will.
Directly after O'Connor concludes that free will cannot exist, Shapiro argues that the analysis equivocates about the self and dissolves the very deciding subject under discussion.
The burden remains with the person asserting free will, because theism's appeal to mystery does not answer the logical objection or transfer the explanatory burden to atheism.
This move challenges Shapiro's claimed explanatory asymmetry and argues that invoking religious mystery cannot insulate an asserted extra-natural faculty from a direct logical objection.
Shapiro's claim that religious mystery is a legitimate escape hatch while materialism bears the burden of explaining agency.
After discussion of an uncaused self and Shapiro's admitted religious escape hatch, O'Connor distinguishes uncertainty from an affirmative claim and assigns the burden to the free-will proponent.

The argument is conditional rather than a proof of God: if people believe in a deciding self, materialism cannot accommodate it, while society nevertheless requires widespread belief in morally weighty choice.
The clarification defines the precise scope of Shapiro's metaphysical claim while reaffirming his motion-level contention that functional social life depends on belief in responsible agency.
O'Connor's assertion that Shapiro affirmatively claims free will and therefore bears the burden of making it intelligible.

Shapiro responds to the burden-of-proof objection by narrowing his thesis to a conditional incompatibility claim, then argues that societies cannot function on universally internalized determinism and nihilism.
If free will is false but civilization depends on believing it, then the socially necessary position—not atheistic disbelief—is the one relying on a delusion.
The concise reversal directly contests the debate's framing by accepting Shapiro's social-utility premise while relocating the alleged delusion to the belief society supposedly needs.
Shapiro's contention that civilization requires belief in free will even if materialist determinism may be true.
As the moderator prepares to end the section, O'Connor combines his denial of free will with Shapiro's social-necessity claim to reverse the accusation of delusion.
Belief in free will is an evolutionarily successful and practically useful fiction whose persistence explains ordinary agency-talk without changing the truth or consequences of determinism.
The answer supplies a secular explanation for the usefulness and resilience of agency beliefs, showing why accepting determinism need not transform conduct or concede extra-natural foundations.
The moderator's formulation of Shapiro's concern that free will may be a necessary fiction protecting people from despair.
Prompted to assess free will as a convenient narrative, O'Connor explains that evolution embedded the experience deeply enough that intellectual rejection rarely alters how people live.
Grounding ethics in a nonexistent divine authority combines human moral fallibility with an authority that adherents regard as immune to human correction.
This directly contests the claim that religion securely grounds morality by arguing that divine attribution can magnify rather than solve moral danger.
Alex develops his opening account of morality by contrasting revisable human compromises with purported divine commands that cannot be countered by ordinary law or reproach.
Religious moral absolutes restrain individual and tribal self-interest, support equal law, and create shared institutions that secular self-interest alone cannot reliably sustain.
The move supplies the principal affirmative mechanism connecting religious belief to morality, universal obligation, institutional trust, and social order.
Alex's claim that alleged divine commands make violent believers uniquely resistant to moral correction.
Ben reframes the comparison around whether religious prohibition or unaided self-interest is more likely to prevent violence, then broadens the case to law and communal institutions.
Removing fundamental moral claims from debate may create cohesion, but it also makes harmful religious imperatives exceptionally difficult to challenge and may not be a worthwhile tradeoff.
This answers the affirmative social-utility mechanism on its own terms by identifying the corresponding cost of placing mistaken norms beyond revision.
Ben's argument that divine moral absolutes check self-interest and provide the shared orientation required for cohesive communities.
Alex grants that religion can promote happiness, family formation, and cohesion, but stresses that the same authoritative force can protect conduct both speakers would reject.
Modern Western moral and scientific achievements often arose through resistance to religious doctrines, so religious traditions cannot straightforwardly claim those achievements as their products.
The argument directly challenges the affirmative historical narrative that secular Western values and scientific progress depend upon inherited Judeo-Christian foundations.
Ben's claim that Western equality, moral outlook, and social institutions derive from a specifically biblical and Judeo-Christian tradition.
Alex contrasts retrospective religious claims over abolition, social justice, and science with scriptural positions and institutional resistance concerning women, slavery, and Galileo.
Judeo-Christian tradition contains reasoned interpretation and internal debate, allowing moral development while preserving common precepts needed for a stable social framework.
This defends religious inheritance against the resistance critique while explaining how tradition can adapt and still furnish shared purpose and social connection.
Alex's contention that abolition, scientific progress, and other Western achievements were won against religious traditions that later appropriated them.
Ben invokes religious participants in abolition and science, presents interpretation as intrinsic to faith, and links religious decline with atomization, low birth rates, and weaker connection.
Any durable society must treat some moral principles as untouchable, and religious authority offers a noncoercive justification strong enough to outweigh personal self-interest.
The move crystallizes the affirmative institutional claim that social order requires authoritative moral commitments whose force exceeds convenience or individual preference.
Alex's argument that divine authority works in both directions, grounding resistance to oppression while also being used to justify oppression.
Ben asks how a society-builder could establish inviolable norms without compulsion and argues that some exceptionally strong authority must overcome citizens' conflicting interests.
The religiosity of early scientists does not establish that science and religion are compatible, because a new method may undermine beliefs only gradually and after its invention.
This contests a major historical warrant for religious scaffolding by separating the founders' inherited beliefs from the later implications of their scientific method.
Ben's reliance on the stated religious commitments of Newton, Galileo, and other scientific pioneers as evidence for religion's role in science.
Alex argues that coercive circumstances obscure Galileo's private convictions and that scientific innovations can erode inherited religion across generations rather than within their founders' lives.
The scientific revolution was positively motivated by religious assumptions that nature is intelligible and the human mind can discover truths embedded in a divinely created universe.
The move provides a causal rather than merely biographical defense of religion's contribution to science and explains doctrinal reinterpretation as compatible with faith.
Alex's claim that the religiosity of scientific pioneers may reflect historical timing and coercive conditions rather than compatibility between science and religion.
Ben points to scientists' avowed search for higher order, identifies intelligibility as a religious premise, and argues that established science can prompt reinterpretation without refuting religion.
Galileo's case shows religion obstructing the immediate fruits of religiously inspired inquiry, because authorities suppressed his scientific conclusion specifically as contrary to scripture.
This tests the affirmative compatibility thesis with a concrete instance in which scriptural authority supplied the stated reason for suppressing scientific findings.
Ben's argument that religious inspiration aided scientific inquiry and that reinterpretation in light of established facts is not a rebuttal of religion.
Alex distinguishes religion's possible motivational utility from its institutional response to discovery, emphasizing Galileo's confinement and the expressly scriptural basis of condemnation.

Although religions must be evaluated specifically, religion generally promotes social cohesion by universalizing identity beyond kinship and sustaining institutions that secular society has not replaced.
This states the broad affirmative social-order case while qualifying the category of religion and identifying cohesion as its strongest general utility argument.

Ben distinguishes better and worse faiths, favors judging lived practice over isolated textual readings, and argues that common supernatural orientation supports universalism, friendship, marriage, and solidarity.
The social consequences of unbelief cannot be inferred from atheism alone because inherited culture, memory, and the particular alternatives substantially determine conduct.
This qualification directly supports the religious side by arguing that apparently successful secular societies may retain inherited religious norms and cannot represent culture-free atheism.
O'Connor's hypothetical comparison between mass conversion to atheism and conversion to Islam.
After repeated requests for specificity, Shapiro distinguishes liberal and fundamentalist Islam and argues that remembered religious culture changes what an atheist society would actually become.
Specific scriptural rules permitting human ownership weaken religion's claim to provide an unquestionable moral authority and may have impeded opposition to slavery.
The move attacks the claimed moral advantage of religious foundations by arguing that authoritative scripture can entrench conduct both participants regard as gravely immoral.
Shapiro's claim that religious practice and interpretive tradition matter more than a decontextualized reading of scripture.
O'Connor accepts that crude literalism can misread a diverse collection of texts, then argues that detailed legal permissions are harder to contextualize away and bear directly on slavery.
Revelation addressed to historically situated people may regulate and gradually humanize a universal institution such as slavery without endorsing it as an timeless ideal.

The response supplies the religious side's principal explanation for morally troubling scripture, preserving divine moral authority by distinguishing timeless truths from historically feasible reforms.
O'Connor's argument that explicit scriptural regulation of slavery made the practice religiously protected and harder to oppose.

Shapiro argues that scripture communicates enduring truths to people within particular historical limits, contains no mandate to own slaves, and can be evaluated against harsher contemporary legal systems.
The accommodation defense fails when scripture abolishes other entrenched practices yet affirmatively permits conquest, enslavement, forced marriage, and selective preservation of captives.
This counterargument challenges the coherence of historically accommodated revelation and contends that the texts contain positive moral wrongs rather than merely incomplete reform.
Shapiro's claim that revelation had to communicate at an attainable historical level and gradually liberalize existing institutions.
O'Connor contrasts slavery with practices scripture condemns outright, then invokes detailed rules of conquest and captivity to argue that the record cannot be explained as humane gradual reform.
Gradual reform is a normal response to entrenched evil, while the Bible also contains universalizing principles that later supported the abolitionist moral tradition.
The move links scriptural moral development to abolition and argues that internal religious principles, rather than secular independence, generated the tradition used to condemn slavery.
O'Connor's claim that biblical conquest and captivity rules constitute affirmative immorality inconsistent with gradual moral improvement.

Shapiro defends gradualism, points to biblical human equality and duties toward strangers, and says apparently conflicting passages require a longstanding interpretive tradition rather than isolated reading.
Calling slavery wrong now but acceptable within its original religious setting makes the supposedly transcendent religious moral foundation look historically relative.
The objection targets an internal tension in the religious case: fixed moral authority is invoked against secular relativism while scriptural permissions are defended through historical change.
Shapiro's assertion that biblical slavery was not considered immoral then and that modern morality developed from Judeo-Christian tradition.
O'Connor asks which side is relativistic when a religious moral system claims immunity from human debate but explains an acknowledged scriptural wrong by reference to its historical acceptance.
A practice can have been objectively wrong in antiquity even if its wrongness became socially recognized only through later development within a religious moral tradition.
This distinction is necessary to defend objective religious morality while conceding that earlier religious societies practiced and regulated conduct now judged immoral.
O'Connor's accusation that historical accommodation of scriptural slavery turns Shapiro's transcendent morality into moral relativism.

Shapiro says slavery was wrong even then, attributes its later condemnation to a developing religious tradition, and asks whether immediate abolition was practicable for historically situated revelation.
Even if wholesale abolition were historically impracticable, scripture could easily have required enslaved families to be released together instead of using separation to secure lifelong servitude.
The example narrows the dispute from complete abolition to a modest feasible reform, challenging the claim that morally troubling permissions were necessary concessions to social conditions.
Shapiro's suggestion that immediate abolition may have been impracticable and that revelation therefore had to move people gradually away from slavery.
O'Connor analyzes the rule governing a Hebrew slave's wife and children, arguing that family release after seven years would have been a limited and nonrevolutionary moral improvement.
Even if religion were socially useful, a convinced atheist cannot choose sincere belief or honestly teach claims considered false merely to obtain religion's practical benefits.
This move directly confronts the motion's proposed religious scaffolding by separating social utility from truth and arguing that secular people must pursue beneficial norms without dishonest belief.
Shapiro's broader argument that religious institutions uniquely sustain family formation, disciplined conduct, social cohesion, and civilizational continuity.

O'Connor proposes encouraging conventional social goods without invoking God, then argues that perceived usefulness cannot produce conviction and would not justify deceiving oneself or one's children.
Religious doubt permits honest presentation of competing views, but durable good conduct still depends on God-centered institutions that provide daily cultural reinforcement and social support.

The closing argument answers the honesty objection while restating the pro side's central claim that individual secular encouragement cannot replace the networks and authority of religious institutions.
O'Connor's argument that unbelievers cannot manufacture sincere faith or responsibly transmit beliefs they regard as false for the sake of social utility.

Shapiro distinguishes certainty from doubt, recommends presenting children with both religious and atheist arguments, and argues that churches embed conduct in supportive culture more effectively than individual advice.
